claims.text: In CrFeCoNiX alloys exposed above 900 °C, high alloy configurational entropy drives formation of a single-phase, homogeneous oxide.
A uniform single-phase oxide accommodates thermal expansion with minimal mismatch stress.
Minimizing thermal-expansion mismatch stress allows the oxide to remain coherent and protective.
Multiphase alloy states have lower effective configurational entropy than single-phase alloy states.
Lower-effective-entropy or multiphase alloys develop heterogeneous oxide scales prone to cracking and spallation.
The alloy's degree of configurational disorder governs the uniformity of cation distribution in the oxide forming on it.
High configurational disorder can stabilize a random, homogeneous, single-phase oxide.
The single-phase oxide has reduced grain-boundary density.
Reduced oxide grain-boundary density lowers internal stress.
Multiple oxide phases and interfaces promote stress concentrations and crack initiation leading to spallation.
Single-phase CrFeCoNiX solid solutions will form continuous, adherent, coherent oxide layers that persist during high-temperature exposure.
Multiphase CrFeCoNiX variants will form nonuniform, cracked oxide scales that spall under the same conditions.
CrFeCoNi without X, or a multiphase variant of similar base composition, is known to form heterogeneous oxides under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
The proposed behavior applies above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
The identity of X as Si, Mn, or Al and the alloy's single- versus multiphase state are critical boundaries governing oxide behavior.
Oxidation kinetics may also contribute to oxide formation and persistence.
Statistically equivalent oxide uniformity, adhesion, and cracking or spallation resistance in controlled single-phase and multiphase samples would falsify the proposed configurational-entropy effect.
